newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands of miners gather in Bonn against cuts.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of miners gather in Bonn against cuts.

text.p: Thousands of miners poured into Bonn overnight and in the early morning for a huge protest as Chancellor Helmut Kohl prepared to meet the miners' union to discuss a government plan to slash coal subsidies.

Police were diverting traffic around Bonn's government quarter, virtually besieged since Monday by angry pitworkers who fear more than half of them will lose their jobs as part of the government's latest move to save money.
Buses poured into Bonn all night from the mining districts of the Ruhr, Germany's ailing steel-and-coal heartland, and from Saar state on the French border.
Union leaders said they expected about 20,000 of Germany's 90,000 miners to turn out in Bonn to continue the protests, while others demonstrated in their home regions.
Some said that if Kohl failed to make concessions in his talks with miners' union leader Hans Berger (eds: starts 1230 GMT, news conference 1500 GMT), the already tense atmosphere could turn violent.

"The mood in Saar is explosive and could be hard to control," said a spokeswoman for the workers' council at Saar Mines, where miners continued to cause traffic chaos by blocking Germany's main motorway and road routes to neighbouring Luxembourg. "I can't rule out violent protests."
The same sentiments could be heard from many of the brawny miners with tattooed arms and smudged faces who spent the night camping out little more than an angry stone's throw from Kohl's chancellery.

But Economics Minister Guenther Rexrodt of the free-market Free Democrats (FDP) said there was little room for compromise when each mining job was costing the government 130,000 marks ($75,000) a year.
"There is no way out of a drastic cut in subsidies in the next few years," he told ARD television late on Monday as the FDP insisted it would not yield to "pressure from the street".

Work in Germany's 18 pits ground to a halt last Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks ($2.2 billion) from nine billion by the year 2005. Miners accuse the government of breaking a promise to phase out aid gradually.
Dozens of pitworkers, keeping themselves warm with sleeping bags and coal-fired braziers, chained themselves overnight to the Bonn headquarters of the FDP, Kohl's junior coalition partners.
The FDP are the driving force behind the cuts and the miners had stopped anyone getting into the building since Monday.
Others spent the night maintaining a blockade of the headquarters of Kohl's Christian Democrats.

But the atmosphere was different at the opposition Social Democratic Party (SPD), which rules the coal states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Saar and which is boycotting tax talks to put pressure on the government to change its coal plans.
The SPD put up around 300 miners in its headquarters, where SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping gave a speech calling the goverment plans a "death sentence" for the mining industry.
Party volunteers organised truckloads of sleeping bags and blankets and prepared hot food and drinks for the miners.
The miners' union IG Bergbau says government plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.
While miners accept their industry's days are numbered, they say a minimum of 6.5 billion marks in subsidies until 2005 is essential to stem spiralling unemployment in mining regions.
But FDP parliamentary economics spokesman Paul Friedhoff said he did not think Kohl would be moved by the protest.
"Berger is speaking for 80,000 miners, Kohl for 80 million citizens, whose money must not be allowed to be used to finance unprofitable jobs any longer," he told Berlin's daily Tageszeitung.
